title: Woke women of the 90s return: Toxic white feminism and the Murphy Brown and Roseanne reboots
author: Amanda Konkle
abstract: Two feminist icons of the 1990s returned to network television in 2018: Murphy Brown and Roseanne Conner. Neither rebooted character survived the reboot's first season. Despite their attempts to demonstrate that they were 'woke,' the acting styles and strong personas of these two icons were, this paper argues, not appealing to a younger generation of television viewers and feminists and, simultaneously, too progressive for the older and more conventional audiences of the networks on which they aired. Moreover, both leading characters demonstrated the narrowmindedness associated with a toxic white feminism that overlooks issues of class and race.
key_findings: Toxic white feminism characterized by narrow-mindedness that overlooks issues of class and race; 1990s feminist icons (Murphy Brown, Roseanne Conner) failed to resonate with contemporary audiences.

title: The Future of Difference: Beyond the Toxic Entanglement of Racism, Sexism and Feminism
author: Sneja Gunew (reviewing Hark & Villa)
abstract: Sabine Hark and Paula-Irene Villa ground their analysis of the complex workings of difference in the example or event of Cologne 2016, when New Year celebrations in the city were marked by the assault of numerous women by numerous men. The analysis traces how this event created an 'emotionally explosive moral node' that gathered toxic politics in its wake, culminating in an unexpected alliance between traditional German feminists and right-wing groups.
key_findings: Cologne 2016 as a pivotal 'node' that toxicologically gathered harmful politics; unexpected alliance formed between traditional German feminists and right-wing groups.

title: Cyborg Feminism and Toxic Colonialism in Chen Qiufan's Waste Tide
author: Yuan Yuan
abstract: Examines the intersection of cyborg feminism and toxic colonialism in Chen Qiufan's science fiction novel Waste Tide.
key_findings: Intersection of cyborg feminism with toxic colonialism themes in contemporary science fiction.

title: The Semantic Shift: Distinguishing Feminism from Misandry in Modern Social Movements
author: Suranya Sengupta
abstract: Feminism is perhaps the most talked-about global movement in the digital world today. However, very few people who claim to be advocates of feminism on digital platforms are aware of the history and journey of the reform for equal rights. The word Feminism did not even exist when the quest for equal rights had started in society. However, with the development and success of many such reforms, Feminism today is a far cry from what it used to be. It is very important that one can distinguish between the ideas of Radical feminism, Liberal feminism and Misandry. But to do that, one must consider the history and purpose of the movement.
key_findings: Need to distinguish between Radical feminism, Liberal feminism and Misandry in modern social movements; contemporary digital feminism diverges significantly from original equal rights goals.

title: The new feminist frontier on community-based learning: popular feminism, online misogyny, and toxic masculinities
author: Rita Basílio de Simões, Inês Amaral, S. Santos
abstract: Feminist activism has always promoted informal learning opportunities for men and women. Internet, along with ICTs, has expanded these opportunities by affording largescale feminist mobilisation and connection. Yet, the digital environment is not only enhancing feminist campaigning but also facilitating the contexts for abusive behaviours to flourish. Departing from the concept of social movement learning, we examine the significance of the large-scale reinvigoration of feminist activism to adult education in tandem with the surge of anti-feminist and misogynist ideas in the digital environment. We argue that just as online social media brought unprecedented opportunities to provide social movement learning, it offered the same tools to misogynists groups, mostly led by a toxic understanding of masculinity.
key_findings: Online platforms provide equal opportunities for feminist activism and toxic masculinity groups; digital environment enables both social movement learning and spread of misogynist ideas; toxic masculinity reinvented through same online tools used by feminists.

title: Feminism and the Horrors of Toxic Masculinity in Pedro Almodóvar's The Skin I Live In (2011)
author: Mason Nagy
abstract: This article analyzes the Spanish horror film The Skin I Live In (TSILI) from a feminist perspective. Different feminist theories such as the male gaze, toxic masculinity, and the Final Girl are used to explore how TSILI criticizes heteronormative masculinity. By comparing Almodóvar's film to other horror classics such as Psycho and Halloween, I discuss how TSILI offers a unique and modernist depiction of gender within horror.
key_findings: The Skin I Live In uses toxic masculinity as a horror element; film critiques heteronormative masculinity through feminist theoretical frameworks.

title: A Less Toxic Feminism: Can the Internet Solve the Age Old Question of How to Put Intersectional Theory into Practice?
author: Fredrika Thelandersson
abstract: Examines whether the internet can facilitate intersectional feminist practice and reduce toxicity in feminist movements.
key_findings: Investigation of internet's potential for implementing intersectional theory in feminism; explores pathways to a less toxic form of feminism.

title: Bros v. Hos: Postfeminism, Anti-feminism and the Toxic Turn in Digital Gender Politics
author: Debbie Ging
abstract: Examines the toxic turn in digital gender politics, focusing on postfeminism and anti-feminism dynamics in online spaces.
key_findings: Postfeminism and anti-feminism contribute to toxic dynamics in digital gender politics; 'Bros v. Hos' phenomenon marks a toxic turn in online gender discourse.

title: Feminism, Surveys, and Toxic Details
author: Various
abstract: Examines toxic dimensions within feminist discourse and survey methodologies related to gender research.
key_findings: Toxic elements present in feminist discourse and survey-based gender research.

title: Toxic Royalty: Feminism and the Rhetoric of Beauty in Disney Princess Films
author: Stephanie X Hu
abstract: Analyzes feminist critiques and toxic beauty standards in Disney princess films.
key_findings: Disney princess films perpetuate toxic beauty standards through feminist lens; rhetoric of beauty intersects with feminist critique.

title: Toxic Feminism: Hope and Hopelessness after Feminism
author: Claire Colebrook
abstract: Explores the paradoxes of toxic feminism and the emotional landscape of hope and hopelessness in post-feminist contexts.
key_findings: Toxic feminism creates paradoxical hope/hopelessness; feminist movement reaches a crisis point after which continuation becomes questionable.

title: Feminism and New Men's Support for Gender Equality
author: Amaliyah Izzul Islam, Ana Kuswanti, Radita Gora Tayinapis, M. Muqsith
abstract: This research examines the concept of 'new men' in the context of feminism and their involvement in supporting gender equality. Although the feminist movement has shown significant progress, men's involvement is still limited due to toxic masculinity and deep-rooted patriarchal norms. This research aims to investigate the new role of men in deconstructing traditional gender roles, especially in domestic and childcare tasks that women often bear.
key_findings: Toxic masculinity and patriarchal norms limit men's involvement in gender equality; 'new men' actively deconstruct traditional gender roles; men's involvement in feminism remains constrained by social stigma and loss of social status.

title: Feminism, Bible, Texts and Terror – A Feminist Reflection
author: Barbara Thiede, Johanna Stiebert
abstract: Forty years on from the publication of Phyllis Trible's pivotal book Texts of Terror (1984), two feminist-identifying Hebrew Bible scholars review feminist commentary on biblical texts of sexual violence arguing that the field remains vibrant, diverse, interdisciplinary, and dynamic.
key_findings: Feminist biblical criticism remains vibrant and dynamic; reading with empathy is critical to feminist project; ongoing need to resist toxic biblical content in context of sexual violence.

title: Beyond Hashtags: Understanding the Perceptions and Impact of Online Feminism among Young Instagram and Twitter Users in the UAE
author: Mohammad Amaan Siddiqui
abstract: Digital feminist literature almost exclusively focuses on specific campaigns, hashtags, trigger events, or dramatic phenomena, understudying everyday feminism's impact beyond feminists and its general reputation among non-elites. Participants perceived and experienced online feminism mostly negatively, citing misdirected aggression, perceived misandry, performative activism, doubts on its feminists' information and goals, and Westernization and Orientalism.
key_findings: Online feminism perceived negatively among UAE youth; perceived misandry cited as a key concern; performative activism and Westernization seen as problems; 'feminism' generally stigmatized in Gulf context.

title: Misinformed Misandry: Ugly Anti-Oil Eco-Feminism
author: M. Stirling
abstract: Critiques anti-oil eco-feminism as a form of misandry that misinforms environmental discourse.
key_findings: Anti-oil eco-feminism characterized as 'misinformed misandry'; intersection of environmental and feminist politics produces problematic discourse.

title: HAS FEMINISM BECOME SCARY?
author: Ruchie Sah
abstract: This paper explores the evolution and shifting perception of feminism from a movement rooted in the pursuit of gender equality to its complex and sometimes controversial interpretation in the society. It traces feminism's journey from the first wave's focus on suffrage to later movements addressing broader issues like bodily autonomy, workplace discrimination, and gender norms. While highlighting feminism's vital role in advocating for women's rights, the paper critically examines how some practices, under the banner of feminism, have sparked debates over fairness, misuse of legal provisions, and emerging concerns around misandry.
key_findings: Feminism's evolution from equal rights movement to controversial force; emergence of misandry concerns; misuse of legal provisions under feminist banner; need to balance advocacy with accountability.

title: Historical and Partisan shifts in Korean press representation of feminism (1990–2022)
author: Dayei Oh, Bokyong Shin
abstract: This study examines how feminist issues have been represented in South Korean press discourse from 1990 to 2022, using a corpus of 49,028 articles. Liberal outlets tend to emphasize structural sexism and misogyny, whereas conservative outlets frame feminism in relation to misandry and electoral and parliamentary politics.
key_findings: Korean press shifted from gender-specific to gender-neutral terminology; thematic transition from structural inequality to gender conflict and controversy; liberal outlets emphasize sexism/misogyny, conservative outlets link feminism to misandry; media depoliticizes feminist discourse.

title: LexiGuard: A Multilingual Transformer-Based Approach to Detecting Sexist and Toxic Language
author: Zuzana Sokolová, Matus Pleva, Eva Kupcová, M. Sokol, Magdaléna Majerčáková
abstract: This paper presents LexiGuard, a multilingual transformer-based system designed for the detection of sexist and toxic language in Slovak and English online communication. A balanced and custom-annotated corpus was created to capture expressions of misogyny, misandry, and neutrality across three levels of toxicity.
key_findings: LexiGuard achieves 89% accuracy for expression type classification and 85% for toxicity classification; model captures both misogyny and misandry; dataset covers low/medium/high toxicity levels in Slovak and English.

title: Wrong Use of Feminism on Social Media Platforms
author: Santanu Tanti
abstract: This work explores the pervasive misappropriation of feminism on social media platforms. It delineates how feminism is often misrepresented, diluted, and commodified for commercial gain, leading to a shallow understanding of its core principles. Furthermore, it discusses the propagation of toxic femininity under the guise of feminism, the polarization of discourse, and the neglect of intersectionality.
key_findings: Feminism misappropriated and commodified on social media; toxic femininity propagates under feminist banner; discourse polarization increases; intersectionality neglected in digital feminist spaces.

title: Gender Stereotypes and Toxic Masculinity: Phenomenological Study of Pamulang University Students
author: Dr. Yunita, S.S. M. Sas
abstract: In Indonesia, which is still considered a conservative country, feminism as a gender-based emancipatory movement has become an understanding that tends to be covered by the glitter of patriarchism. Resistance to feminist thought is quite massive because the majority of people consider it to be a Western epistemology that is not in harmony with Eastern cultural values.
key_findings: Feminism faces massive resistance in conservative Indonesian context; perceived as Western epistemology incompatible with Eastern values; toxic masculinity recognized by students; gender stereotypes remain pervasive.
